selected.title: The Leasing Agent Called About Our Second Apartment
selected.hook: A leasing agent called to ask when I wanted the keys to an apartment I'd never seen.
selected.voiceover:
A leasing agent called to ask when I wanted the keys to an apartment I'd never seen.

She had my name, my phone number, and my boyfriend listed as the other tenant. We already lived together, so I assumed it was some weird mistake.

Then she mentioned the building.

For months, my boyfriend had been showing me photos of that exact place, saying maybe we could afford something like it next year.

I asked the agent when the application was submitted.

Three weeks ago.

When I called him, he admitted he'd rented it, but said it was supposed to be a surprise. Our current lease ends in four months, and apparently he'd decided we'd move early.

That sounded almost romantic until I asked how my name got on the application.

He'd uploaded copies of documents I'd sent him last year when we applied for our current apartment. He'd also paid the deposit from our joint emergency account.

Then came the part that really bothered me.

The new apartment was forty minutes farther from my job, but five minutes from his.

He'd already measured our furniture, booked movers, and told his parents our moving date.

Everyone knew except me.

He keeps saying he was trying to build our future and that I'm ruining a thoughtful surprise over paperwork.

But a surprise is dinner or a weekend away. This was a lease, our savings, and my commute decided without me.

Would you forgive the intention, or is making a decision this big alone the real problem?

A leasing agent calls about an apartment she never applied for, only to reveal that her boyfriend has been planning their move in secret. What first sounds like an elaborate romantic surprise quickly becomes a relationship drama about shared savings, consent, commuting, and who gets to make major decisions for a couple. Would the intention matter to you?
